listenAndRepeat.scenarioTitle: Getting the Kitchen Ready for the Potluck
listenAndRepeat.scenarioDescription: Listen to an older sibling walk a younger sibling through kitchen setup before a shared potluck meal, and repeat what the sibling says. Repeat only once.

image.prompt:
FLAT VECTOR INFOGRAPHIC ILLUSTRATION, one square image.

VIEW: elevated three-quarter "illustrated map" view of the whole location at once, quasi-isometric — the ground/floor is drawn as flattened foreshortened shapes seen from above at an angle, while furniture, equipment and people are drawn in near-side elevation. The entire setting is visible in one frame, like a hand-drawn guide map of the place.

COLOR — this is the most important rule. The environment is STRICTLY GRAYSCALE / ACHROMATIC: near-white background (#FAFAFA), pale gray surfaces (#E6E6E6), mid grays (#D2D2D2, #C8C8C8), darker gray for the nearest foreground (#A0A0A0), and dark gray to near-black line work (#505050). NO color anywhere in the environment — no blue, no green, no brown floors, no colored walls. This applies without exception to things that are normally colored: WATER AND SWIMMING POOLS ARE GRAY, NOT BLUE OR CYAN; glass is gray; plants, trees and grass are gray, not green; sky is near-white.

SPOT COLOR: exactly one accent hue, a soft muted teal (#00A082), used ONLY as a rounded organic highlight blob sitting behind and hugging the silhouette of each KEY OBJECT listed below, making those objects pop out of the gray scene. The key objects themselves may be muted golden-tan (#FABE50) or rust brown (#965A32). Nothing else in the picture carries any hue.

LINE: crisp, clean, uniform thin line weight throughout, like a printed vector diagram rather than a pencil sketch. Every surface is a COMPLETELY FLAT FILL of one single solid tone — NO gradients, NO soft shading, NO drop shadows, NO ambient occlusion, NO texture, NO hatching, NO photorealism, NO 3D rendering. Depth is conveyed only by stacking flat bands of different gray tones.

PEOPLE: a few small, simple, FACELESS grayscale figures in candid poses — plain oval heads with no facial features at all, no skin tone, no clothing color.

FRAMING: the illustration sits inside a thin black rectangular border with a generous clean margin. Uncluttered and airy, not crowded.

ABSOLUTELY NO TEXT: no letters, no words, no numbers, no labels, no captions, no signage text, no logos, no watermarks, no arrows. Any sign must be blank or a wordless pictogram only.

SCENE TO ILLUSTRATE: Getting the Kitchen Ready for the Potluck. Listen to an older sibling walk a younger sibling through kitchen setup before a shared potluck meal, and repeat what the sibling says. Repeat only once.

Draw the location as a single connected scene. These are the KEY OBJECTS and areas that must be clearly visible and individually recognizable, each marked with the teal highlight blob:
- Let's wipe the counters clean first.
- Grab the sponge and the spray cleaner under the sink.
- Then clear a shelf in the fridge for the shared dishes.
- You can rinse the bowls, but leave the lids in the drawer.
- After you finish the counters, preheat the oven for the last dish.
- Carry the folding table and set it up near the door before guests arrive.
- The table you carried over is where the guests will set down their dishes.

Depict the physical places and things named above (the counter, the doors, the rooms, the equipment) as recognizable drawn objects in their spatial relationship to each other. Do not write any of these words in the image — show them as pictures only.

interview.scenarioTitle: A Call From the Local History Archive
interview.intro: You will now take a phone call from a local history archivist who collects brief, unscheduled interviews about family traditions. Answer each question as naturally as you can. You will have 45 seconds to respond to each question.

questions.question: Thank you for taking the time to speak with me today. I'm collecting stories about family traditions for the local archive. Could you tell me about one tradition your family has kept, and roughly how long it's been part of your family?
Great, thank you. Now think back to the most recent time you took part in that tradition. What happened, and who was there with you?

That's a great memory. Some people believe family traditions should stay exactly the way they've always been. Others think it's fine for traditions to change and adapt over time. Which view is closer to yours, and why?

Good points. Let me ask you one final question. Many family traditions fade as older generations pass them down less often. Do you think families should make more effort to record these traditions before they disappear, and what might happen if they don't?

fridge shelf cleared for shared dishes
oven preheated for the last dish
folding table set up near the door

interview.topic: a family tradition kept and passed down at home
interview.premise: a local history archivist makes brief unprepared phone calls asking residents about one tradition their family has kept over time
questionArc: Ask which specific family tradition the person keeps and roughly how long it has been part of their family, a concrete retrievable fact.
Ask the person to recall the most recent time they took part in that tradition and who was there with them.
Present two contrasting views on whether traditions should stay exactly as they've always been or should adapt over time, and ask the person to take a side.
Broaden to whether families should make more effort to record fading traditions before they disappear, inviting a prediction or recommendation.
